title: Meeting Rooms II — Minimum Rooms Required
prompt: Given an array of meeting time intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], return the minimum number of conference rooms required so that no two meetings sharing a room overlap. A meeting that starts exactly when another ends does NOT conflict (touching endpoints can share a room).
blurb: The maximum-overlap problem — a min-heap of end times reuses rooms as meetings finish, or split start/end events into a sweep line and track the running peak.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Reframes 'minimum rooms' as 'maximum number of meetings overlapping at any instant', and clarifies the touching-endpoint rule (end == start does not conflict).

rubric.label: Approach
rubric.description: Reaches the min-heap of end times (sort by start, reuse a room when the earliest-ending meeting has finished) OR the sweep-line with separate sorted start/end arrays tracking a running counter. Recognizes counting overlaps, not pairwise checks.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: Heap: sort by start; for each meeting, if the min end <= current start, pop (reuse) before pushing; heap size is the answer. Sweep: two-pointer over sorted starts/ends, increment on start, decrement when start >= end, track peak. Handles the touching case with the right inequality.

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting (and heap ops are log n). O(n) space for the heap / event arrays. Contrasts with the O(n^2) pairwise-overlap counting.

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: Clean sort + single heap, or clean two-pointer sweep; the reuse condition and peak tracking are readable and not buried in special cases.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Empty input (0), single meeting (1), all meetings identical (n rooms), fully nested meetings, back-to-back touching meetings sharing one room, all-disjoint (1 room).

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Tests the touching-endpoint case ([[0,5],[5,10]] -> 1) and a heavy-overlap case, verifying the reuse condition uses the correct <= vs <.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Explains the max-overlap reframing and why sorting by start plus a min-heap on ends correctly models room reuse.

constraints: A meeting starting exactly when another ends does NOT overlap (they can share a room)

examples.explanation: [0,30] runs the whole time. [5,10] overlaps it, needing a 2nd room. [15,20] starts after [5,10] ends at 10, so it reuses that room. Peak overlap is 2.
The two meetings do not overlap ([2,4] ends before [7,10] starts), so a single room suffices.

test_cases.expected: 1 — touching endpoints do not conflict; the second reuses the room freed at 5
3 — three simultaneous identical meetings need three rooms
2 — [1,13] and [6,9] overlap; [13,15] reuses the room freed exactly at 13

reference.optimal_time: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; heap operations are O(log n) each
reference.optimal_space: O(n) — the heap or the start/end event arrays

approaches.name: brute force (count overlaps per meeting)
approaches.idea: For each meeting, count how many others overlap it, or check every pair. The maximum simultaneous overlap is the answer, but computing it pairwise is quadratic.

approaches.name: min-heap of end times
approaches.idea: Sort meetings by start time. Maintain a min-heap of end times of meetings currently occupying rooms. For each meeting in start order: if the heap's smallest end time is <= this meeting's start, that room is free — pop it (reuse). Then push this meeting's end time. The heap's size at any point is the rooms in use; its maximum size is the answer (in practice, its final size after the reuse-then-push discipline).

approaches.name: sweep-line / chronological events
approaches.idea: Separate all start times and all end times into two sorted arrays. Two-pointer walk: if starts[i] < ends[j], a meeting begins -> rooms++, i++ and update peak; else a meeting has ended -> rooms--, j++. Using starts[i] < ends[j] (strict) frees the room on a touching endpoint. The peak of rooms is the answer. Equivalent to +1/-1 events sorted by time.

follow_ups: Return WHICH meetings share each room (an actual assignment), not just the count — assign each reused room an id and track it on the heap.
Meeting Rooms I — can a single person attend all meetings (any overlap at all)? Sort by start and check adjacent pairs; O(n log n).
Maximum number of non-overlapping meetings you can schedule in one room (activity selection) — greedy by earliest end time.
Streaming meetings arriving online — maintain rooms with an interval tree / balanced BST keyed by time.
Weighted variant: maximize total value of non-conflicting meetings in k rooms — DP / min-cost flow territory.
reference.reference_solution:
Min-heap: minMeetingRooms(intervals): if not intervals: return 0. sort intervals by start ascending. heap = []  // min-heap of end times. for (s, e) in intervals: if heap and heap[0] <= s: heappop(heap)  // earliest-ending room is free (<= allows touching reuse). heappush(heap, e). return len(heap). The heap[0] <= s test is the correctness crux: <= lets a meeting starting exactly when another ends reuse the room; using < would over-allocate on touching endpoints.

Sweep-line alternative: starts = sorted(s for s,e in intervals); ends = sorted(e for s,e in intervals); i = j = rooms = peak = 0. while i < n: if starts[i] < ends[j]: rooms += 1; peak = max(peak, rooms); i += 1. else: rooms -= 1; j += 1. return peak. Both are O(n log n) from the sort; choose whichever framing you can explain most cleanly.
pitfalls: Wrong inequality on the touching case: using < instead of <= (heap) or <= instead of < (sweep) over-allocates a room for back-to-back meetings.
Forgetting to sort by start before the heap pass.
Pushing before checking/popping the freed room, so the heap never shrinks and every meeting looks concurrent.
Sorting starts and ends TOGETHER instead of independently in the sweep-line version, which loses the ability to reuse rooms.
O(n^2) pairwise overlap counting when the input can be 10^4 meetings.

interviewer_notes: The reframing 'minimum rooms == maximum simultaneous overlap' is the key conceptual step — a candidate who states it up front is signaling well. First clarifying signal: do they ask about the touching-endpoint rule? If not, let them assume, then challenge with [[0,5],[5,10]] during testing — this exposes whether their inequality is right. Reaching either the min-heap or the sweep-line is the mid bar. Stay silent through implementation; nudge only if they attempt pairwise overlap counting (ask 'what if there are 10,000 meetings?'). Watch the pop-before-push ordering in the heap version. Once correct, escalate to returning the actual room assignment (which meetings go where), or contrast with Meeting Rooms I and activity-selection to test whether they see the family of interval problems. If they breeze through, ask for the streaming/online variant to surface interval-tree thinking.
